title: Meru Millet Porridge
author: Mama Wanjiru

heritage.origin: Meru County — Eastern Kenya, slopes of Mount Kenya
heritage.history: The Meru people inhabit the fertile slopes of Mount Kenya. Their millet porridge has a slightly thicker consistency and the traditional addition of honey from the region's renowned honey-producing communities. The Meru have cultivated finger millet on Mount Kenya's slopes for generations.
heritage.modernEvolution: Meru millet porridge continues as a daily breakfast tradition and is valued for its nutritional profile.

desc: Meru Millet Porridge — thick, nourishing finger millet porridge prepared the traditional Meru way — slightly thicker than standard uji and sweetened with local Meru honey. The daily breakfast of the Mount Kenya slopes.
longDesc: The Meru version of millet porridge is notably thicker than standard Kenyan uji. It is sweetened with the honey from Meru's renowned honey trees and eaten with a spoon.
ingredients: 2—3 tbsp Meru honey or any raw honey
½ cup milk — optional for creaminess
steps: Mix millet flour with 1 cup cold water to a smooth slurry.
Bring remaining 2 cups of water to a boil.
Pour slurry into boiling water, stirring continuously.
Stir over medium heat for 8—10 minutes until thick — Meru uji is notably thicker than standard.
Remove from heat. Add honey — honey added off the heat preserves its live enzymes.
chefTips: Adding honey after removing from heat preserves its natural enzymes.
The Meru version is thicker than standard uji.
Raw, unprocessed Meru honey is incomparably better here.
commonMistakes: Too thin — the Meru tradition produces thick, spoonable porridge.
cookingScience: Raw honey contains enzymes denatured above 40°C. Adding honey to warm but not boiling porridge preserves these beneficial enzymes.
sustainabilityTips: Meru is renowned for its honey — supporting local beekeepers who maintain native bee colonies.
reheating: Warm gently with a splash of water.
culturalNote: Meru millet porridge reflects the deep agricultural and apicultural traditions of the Mount Kenya slopes — a region producing the world's finest finger millet and extraordinary honey.
